chapters.title: Chemical Reactions and Equations
chapters.overview: The chapter shows how to recognise that a chemical reaction has taken place (change in state, colour, temperature or evolution of a gas) and how to represent reactions by word-equations and balanced chemical equations with state symbols. It classifies reactions as combination, decomposition, displacement, double displacement and oxidation-reduction (redox), and introduces exothermic and endothermic reactions. It ends with the everyday effects of oxidation: corrosion and rancidity.

sections.title: Chemical Reactions and Equations
points: Everyday situations such as milk souring, rusting, fermentation, cooking, digestion and respiration change the nature and identity of the initial substance; whenever a chemical change occurs a chemical reaction has taken place.
Burning magnesium ribbon gives white magnesium oxide powder; lead nitrate with potassium iodide and zinc with dilute acid are also used as activities.
A chemical reaction can be recognised by a change in state, a change in colour, evolution of a gas or a change in temperature.

sections.title: CHEMICAL EQUATIONS
points: A reaction described in a sentence can be written more briefly as a word-equation, e.g. Magnesium + Oxygen → Magnesium oxide.
Substances that undergo chemical change are reactants; the new substance formed is the product.

Reactants are written on the left-hand side (LHS) and products on the right-hand side (RHS), with plus signs between them; the arrowhead points towards the products and shows the direction of the reaction.

subsections.title: Writing a Chemical Equation
points: Chemical equations become concise and useful when chemical formulae replace words, e.g. Mg + O2 → MgO.
If the number of atoms of each element is not the same on both sides, the equation is unbalanced; such an equation is a skeletal chemical equation.

subsections.title: Balanced Chemical Equations
points: By the law of conservation of mass, the number of atoms of each element must be the same before and after a reaction, so skeletal equations must be balanced.
Zn + H2SO4 → ZnSO4 + H2 is already balanced; Fe + H2O → Fe3O4 + H2 is balanced step by step.

Steps: draw boxes around formulae and do not change anything inside them; list atoms of each element; start with the compound with the most atoms (Fe3O4, oxygen); balance hydrogen, then iron; check the final equation 3Fe + 4H2O → Fe3O4 + 4H2.
Formulae cannot be altered while balancing (4 H2O, not H2O4 or (H2O)4); this method using smallest whole-number coefficients is the hit-and-trial method.
Step VII: physical states are shown as (g), (l), (aq) and (s); (aq) means a solution in water; reaction conditions such as temperature, pressure or catalyst may be written above or below the arrow.

sections.title: TYPES OF CHEMICAL REACTIONS
points: During a chemical reaction atoms of one element do not change into another, nor do atoms disappear or appear.
Chemical reactions involve the breaking and making of bonds between atoms to produce new substances.

subsections.title: Combination Reaction
points: Calcium oxide (quick lime) reacts vigorously with water to form slaked lime, calcium hydroxide, releasing much heat.
A reaction in which a single product is formed from two or more reactants is a combination reaction; examples are burning of coal and formation of water from hydrogen and oxygen.
Reactions in which heat is released along with products are exothermic; examples are burning of natural gas, respiration and decomposition of vegetable matter into compost.
Slaked lime used for whitewashing reacts slowly with carbon dioxide in air to form a shiny layer of calcium carbonate (the formula of marble is also CaCO3).

subsections.title: Decomposition Reaction
points: Heating green ferrous sulphate crystals gives ferric oxide, sulphur dioxide and sulphur trioxide; a single reactant breaking into simpler products is a decomposition reaction.
Decomposition carried out by heating is thermal decomposition, e.g. calcium carbonate to calcium oxide (used in cement) and carbon dioxide, and lead nitrate giving brown nitrogen dioxide fumes.

Electrolysis of water gives hydrogen and oxygen at the electrodes; white silver chloride turns grey in sunlight as it decomposes into silver and chlorine, and silver bromide behaves the same way, which is used in black and white photography.
Decomposition reactions need energy as heat, light or electricity; reactions in which energy is absorbed are endothermic.

subsections.title: Displacement Reaction
points: Iron nails in copper sulphate solution become brownish and the blue colour fades because iron displaces copper: Fe + CuSO4 → FeSO4 + Cu.
Zinc and lead also displace copper from its compounds because they are more reactive than copper.

subsections.title: Double Displacement Reaction
points: Mixing sodium sulphate and barium chloride solutions forms a white insoluble substance, barium sulphate, and sodium chloride stays in solution.
An insoluble substance formed is a precipitate, and a reaction producing one is a precipitation reaction.
Reactions in which there is an exchange of ions between the reactants are double displacement reactions.

subsections.title: Oxidation and Reduction
points: Heating copper powder coats it with black copper(II) oxide as oxygen is added; passing hydrogen over the heated CuO reverses this and gives copper.
A substance that gains oxygen is oxidised; one that loses oxygen is reduced.
Reactions in which one reactant is oxidised and another reduced are oxidation-reduction or redox reactions, e.g. ZnO + C → Zn + CO and MnO2 + 4HCl → MnCl2 + 2H2O + Cl2.
Gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen is oxidation; loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen is reduction.

sections.title: HAVE YOU OBSERVED THE EFFECTS OF OXIDATION REACTIONS IN EVERYDAY LIFE?
points: Oxidation reactions have visible effects in daily life, such as corrosion of metals and rancidity of food.

subsections.title: Corrosion
points: Iron articles get coated with a reddish brown powder over time, which is rusting; copper gets a green coating and silver a black coating.
When a metal is attacked by substances around it such as moisture and acids, it corrodes; the process is corrosion.
Corrosion damages car bodies, bridges, iron railings and ships, and much money is spent every year replacing damaged iron.

subsections.title: Rancidity
points: When fats and oils are oxidised they become rancid and their smell and taste change.
Antioxidants are added to foods with fats and oil, air-tight containers slow oxidation, and bags of chips are flushed with nitrogen to prevent oxidation.

bookSummary: A complete chemical equation represents the reactants, products and their physical states symbolically.

A chemical equation is balanced so that the numbers of atoms of each type involved in a chemical reaction are the same on the reactant and product sides of the equation. Equations must always be balanced.
In a combination reaction two or more substances combine to form a new single substance.
Decomposition reactions are opposite to combination reactions. In a decomposition reaction, a single substance decomposes to give two or more substances.
Reactions in which heat is given out along with the products are called exothermic reactions.
Reactions in which energy is absorbed are known as endothermic reactions.
When an element displaces another element from its compound, a displacement reaction occurs.
Two different atoms or groups of atoms (ions) are exchanged in double displacement reactions.
Precipitation reactions produce insoluble salts.
Reactions also involve the gain or loss of oxygen or hydrogen by substances. Oxidation is the gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen. Reduction is the loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen.

chapters.title: Acids, Bases and Salts
chapters.overview: The chapter studies the chemical properties of acids and bases: their reactions with metals, carbonates, each other (neutralisation) and oxides, and shows that acids produce H+(aq) ions and bases OH-(aq) ions in water. It introduces the pH scale and the importance of pH in everyday life, then describes families of salts, the pH of salts, chemicals made from common salt (sodium hydroxide, bleaching powder, baking soda, washing soda) and water of crystallisation, including Plaster of Paris.

sections.title: Acids, Bases and Salts
points: Acids are sour and turn blue litmus red; bases are bitter and turn red litmus blue.
Litmus and turmeric are natural indicators; methyl orange and phenolphthalein are synthetic indicators.
A curry stain on white cloth turns reddish-brown when basic soap is scrubbed on it and yellow again when washed with water.
Litmus is a purple dye extracted from lichen; red cabbage leaves, turmeric and coloured petals of Hydrangea, Petunia and Geranium are also acid-base indicators.

sections.title: UNDERSTANDING THE CHEMICAL PROPERTIES OF ACIDS AND BASES
points: Indicators tell whether a substance is acidic or basic by a change in colour; olfactory indicators change odour in acidic or basic media.

subsections.title: Acids and Bases in the Laboratory
points: Solutions of HCl, H2SO4, HNO3, CH3COOH, NaOH, Ca(OH)2, KOH, Mg(OH)2 and NH4OH are tested with red litmus, blue litmus, phenolphthalein and methyl orange.
Onion-treated cloth strips, vanilla essence and clove oil are tested with dilute HCl and NaOH to see which act as olfactory indicators.

subsections.title: How do Acids and Bases React with Metals?
points: Zinc granules with dilute sulphuric acid give a gas that forms bubbles in soap solution and burns; the gas is hydrogen.
The metal displaces hydrogen from the acid as hydrogen gas and forms a salt: Acid + Metal → Salt + Hydrogen gas.
Zinc warmed with sodium hydroxide solution also gives hydrogen and sodium zincate, but such reactions are not possible with all metals.

subsections.title: How do Metal Carbonates and Metal Hydrogencarbonates React with Acids?
points: Sodium carbonate and sodium hydrogencarbonate react with dilute HCl to give sodium chloride, water and carbon dioxide.
Carbon dioxide turns lime water milky by forming a white precipitate of calcium carbonate; excess CO2 forms soluble calcium hydrogencarbonate.
Limestone, chalk and marble are forms of calcium carbonate; all metal carbonates and hydrogencarbonates react with acids to give salt, carbon dioxide and water.

subsections.title: How do Acids and Bases React with each other?
points: Pink phenolphthalein in NaOH solution loses its colour on adding HCl and the pink reappears on adding more NaOH, showing an acid and base nullify each other.
The reaction between an acid and a base to give a salt and water is a neutralisation reaction: Base + Acid → Salt + Water.

subsections.title: Reaction of Metallic Oxides with Acids
points: Copper oxide dissolves in dilute HCl giving a blue-green solution of copper(II) chloride.
Metal oxide + Acid → Salt + Water; because this resembles a base reacting with an acid, metallic oxides are basic oxides.

subsections.title: Reaction of a Non-metallic Oxide with Base
points: Calcium hydroxide reacts with carbon dioxide to produce a salt and water, like a base reacting with an acid.
Hence non-metallic oxides are acidic in nature.

sections.title: WHAT DO ALL ACIDS AND ALL BASES HAVE IN COMMON?
points: Solutions of HCl and H2SO4 make a bulb glow in a circuit, but glucose and alcohol solutions do not conduct electricity.
Current is carried through acidic solutions by ions; acids contain H+ as cation, so acids produce hydrogen ions H+(aq) in solution, which are responsible for their acidic properties.

subsections.title: What Happens to an Acid or a Base in a Water Solution?
points: HCl gas prepared from NaCl and concentrated sulphuric acid changes wet but not dry blue litmus, so H+ ions from HCl form only in the presence of water.
Hydrogen ions cannot exist alone; they combine with water and are shown as H+(aq) or hydronium ion H3O+.
Bases generate hydroxide (OH-) ions in water; bases soluble in water are alkalis, which are soapy, bitter and corrosive.
Neutralisation can be seen as H+(aq) + OH-(aq) → H2O(l).

Dissolving an acid or base in water is highly exothermic, so acid must always be added slowly to water with constant stirring; mixing with water lowers the concentration of ions per unit volume, which is dilution.

sections.title: HOW STRONG ARE ACID OR BASE SOLUTIONS?
points: A universal indicator is a mixture of several indicators showing different colours at different hydrogen ion concentrations.
The pH scale measures hydrogen ion concentration, generally from 0 (very acidic) to 14 (very alkaline); p stands for 'potenz', German for power.
Higher hydronium ion concentration means lower pH; a neutral solution has pH 7, below 7 is acidic, and rising pH from 7 to 14 means increasing OH- concentration.
Acids giving more H+ ions are strong acids and those giving fewer are weak acids; hydrochloric and acetic acid of the same concentration produce different amounts of H+ ions.

subsections.title: Importance of pH in Everyday Life
points: Our body works within pH 7.0 to 7.8; rain water with pH below 5.6 is acid rain, which lowers river pH and makes aquatic life difficult.
Plants need a specific soil pH range for healthy growth, which can be checked by testing a soil filtrate with universal indicator paper.
The stomach produces hydrochloric acid for digestion; excess acid in indigestion is neutralised by antacids such as magnesium hydroxide (milk of magnesia).
Tooth decay starts when mouth pH falls below 5.5, corroding enamel of calcium hydroxyapatite; basic toothpastes neutralise excess acid.
A bee-sting leaves an acid relieved by baking soda; nettle stinging hair inject methanoic acid, traditionally treated by rubbing with a dock leaf.

sections.title: MORE ABOUT SALTS
points: Salts formed in various reactions are studied for their preparation, properties and uses.

subsections.title: Family of Salts
points: Salts having the same positive or negative radicals belong to a family.
NaCl and Na2SO4 belong to the family of sodium salts; NaCl and KCl belong to the family of chloride salts.

subsections.title: pH of Salts
points: Salts of a strong acid and a strong base are neutral with pH 7.
Salts of a strong acid and weak base are acidic (pH less than 7); salts of a strong base and weak acid are basic (pH more than 7).

subsections.title: Chemicals from Common Salt
points: Sodium chloride is separated from seawater; brown rock salt deposits formed when ancient seas dried up and are mined like coal. Salt was a symbol in the Dandi March.
Electrolysis of brine is the chlor-alkali process: 2NaCl + 2H2O → 2NaOH + Cl2 + H2, with chlorine at the anode, hydrogen at the cathode and NaOH near the cathode.
Bleaching powder, Ca(ClO)2, is made by the action of chlorine on dry slaked lime; it bleaches cotton, linen, wood pulp and laundry, is an oxidising agent and makes drinking water germ-free.

Baking soda (sodium hydrogencarbonate) is made from NaCl, water, CO2 and ammonia; it is a mild non-corrosive base used in baking powder (with tartaric acid), antacids and soda-acid fire extinguishers.
Washing soda, Na2CO3.10H2O, is obtained by recrystallising sodium carbonate; it is used in glass, soap and paper industries, to make borax, for cleaning and for removing permanent hardness of water.

subsections.title: Are the Crystals of Salts really Dry?
points: Heating blue copper sulphate crystals removes water and the salt turns white; adding water restores the blue colour.
Water of crystallisation is the fixed number of water molecules in one formula unit of a salt; copper sulphate has five (CuSO4.5H2O) and gypsum has two (CaSO4.2H2O).
Heating gypsum at 373 K gives calcium sulphate hemihydrate, Plaster of Paris, which sets back to hard gypsum on mixing with water.
Plaster of Paris supports fractured bones and is used for toys, decoration materials and smoothing surfaces; half a water molecule means two formula units share one water molecule.

Acidic nature of a substance is due to the formation of H+(aq) ions in solution. Formation of OH-(aq) ions in solution is responsible for the basic nature of a substance.
When an acid reacts with a metal, hydrogen gas is evolved and a corresponding salt is formed.
When a base reacts with a metal, along with the evolution of hydrogen gas a salt is formed which has a negative ion composed of the metal and oxygen.
When an acid reacts with a metal carbonate or metal hydrogencarbonate, it gives the corresponding salt, carbon dioxide gas and water.
Acidic and basic solutions in water conduct electricity because they produce hydrogen and hydroxide ions respectively.
The strength of an acid or an alkali can be tested by using a scale called the pH scale (0-14) which gives the measure of hydrogen ion concentration in a solution.
A neutral solution has a pH of exactly 7, while an acidic solution has a pH less than 7 and a basic solution a pH more than 7.
Living beings carry out their metabolic activities within an optimal pH range.
Mixing concentrated acids or bases with water is a highly exothermic process.
Acids and bases neutralise each other to form corresponding salts and water.
Water of crystallisation is the fixed number of water molecules present in one formula unit of a salt.
Salts have various uses in everyday life and in industries.

chapters.title: Metals and Non-metals
chapters.overview: The chapter compares the physical properties of metals and non-metals and their exceptions, then studies the chemical properties of metals: reactions with oxygen, water, acids and salt solutions, leading to the reactivity series. It explains how metals and non-metals react by transferring electrons to form ionic compounds and describes their properties. It then covers the occurrence and extraction of metals by reactivity (enrichment, roasting, calcination, reduction, electrolysis, refining), and corrosion and its prevention including alloys.

sections.title: PHYSICAL PROPERTIES
points: Grouping substances can start by comparing their physical properties, using samples such as iron, copper, aluminium, magnesium, sodium, lead and zinc.

subsections.title: Metals
points: Pure metals have a shining surface, called metallic lustre; metals are generally hard, though hardness varies.
Metals can be beaten into thin sheets (malleability; gold and silver are the most malleable) and drawn into wires (ductility; about 2 km of wire can be drawn from one gram of gold).
Metals are good conductors of heat with high melting points; silver and copper are the best conductors, lead and mercury comparatively poor.
Metals conduct electricity, and those that produce a sound on striking a hard surface are sonorous, which is why school bells are made of metal.

subsections.title: Non-metals
points: There are very few non-metals compared with metals, e.g. carbon, sulphur, iodine, oxygen, hydrogen; they are solids or gases except bromine, a liquid.
Elements cannot be grouped by physical properties alone because of exceptions: mercury is a liquid metal; gallium and caesium melt on the palm; iodine is a lustrous non-metal.
Carbon exists as allotropes: diamond is the hardest natural substance with a very high melting point, and graphite conducts electricity.
Alkali metals (lithium, sodium, potassium) are soft enough to cut with a knife and have low densities and melting points.
Burning magnesium gives a basic oxide and burning sulphur gives an acidic one; most non-metals produce acidic oxides and most metals basic oxides.

sections.title: CHEMICAL PROPERTIES OF METALS
points: The chemical properties of metals are studied through their reactions with air, water, acids and solutions of other metal salts.

subsections.title: What happens when Metals are burnt in Air?
points: Almost all metals combine with oxygen to form metal oxides, e.g. copper forms black copper(II) oxide and aluminium forms aluminium oxide.
Metal oxides are basic, but aluminium oxide and zinc oxide react with both acids and bases to give salts and water; these are amphoteric oxides.
Most metal oxides are insoluble in water, but sodium and potassium oxides dissolve to form alkalis.

Potassium and sodium react so vigorously that they are kept in kerosene; magnesium, aluminium, zinc and lead have a protective oxide layer; iron filings burn in a flame; silver and gold do not react with oxygen even at high temperatures.
Anodising forms a thick protective oxide layer on aluminium by making it the anode in electrolysis with dilute sulphuric acid.

subsections.title: What happens when Metals react with Water?
points: Metals react with water to give a metal oxide and hydrogen; soluble metal oxides then form metal hydroxides.
Potassium and sodium react violently with cold water and the hydrogen catches fire; calcium reacts less violently and floats because hydrogen bubbles stick to it.
Magnesium reacts with hot water, not cold; aluminium, iron and zinc react only with steam to form oxides and hydrogen.
Lead, copper, silver and gold do not react with water at all.

subsections.title: What happens when Metals react with Acids?
points: Metals react with dilute acids to give a salt and hydrogen; with dilute HCl reactivity decreases in the order Mg > Al > Zn > Fe, and copper does not react.
Hydrogen is not evolved with nitric acid because HNO3 is a strong oxidising agent that oxidises H2 to water, except that Mg and Mn give H2 with very dilute HNO3.
Aqua regia, a 3:1 mixture of concentrated hydrochloric and nitric acids, can dissolve gold and platinum.

subsections.title: How do Metals react with Solutions of other Metal Salts?
points: An iron nail in copper sulphate solution reacts, but copper wire in iron sulphate solution does not.
Reactive metals displace less reactive metals from their compounds in solution or molten form: Metal A + Salt solution of B → Salt solution of A + Metal B.
Displacement reactions give better evidence about the reactivity of metals than reactions with oxygen, water or acids.

subsections.title: The Reactivity Series
points: The reactivity series is a list of metals arranged in order of decreasing activity, developed from displacement experiments.
The order is K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Pb, [H], Cu, Hg, Ag, Au, from most to least reactive.

sections.title: HOW DO METALS AND NON-METALS REACT?
points: Noble gases with a completely filled valence shell show little chemical activity, so reactivity is explained as a tendency to attain a completely filled valence shell.

Sodium (2,8,1) loses one electron to form Na+ and chlorine (2,8,7) gains one to form Cl-; the oppositely charged ions are held by strong electrostatic forces as sodium chloride, which exists as aggregates of ions, not molecules.
Magnesium loses two electrons to form Mg2+, which combines with two chloride ions to form magnesium chloride.
Compounds formed by transfer of electrons from a metal to a non-metal are ionic or electrovalent compounds.

subsections.title: Properties of Ionic Compounds
points: Physical nature: ionic compounds are solids, somewhat hard because of strong attraction between ions, and generally brittle.
Melting and boiling points: they are high because much energy is needed to break the strong inter-ionic attraction (e.g. NaCl melts at 1074 K).
Solubility: they are generally soluble in water and insoluble in kerosene, petrol, etc.
Conduction of electricity: they conduct in solution and in the molten state, where ions move, but not as solids because the rigid structure stops ions moving.

sections.title: OCCURRENCE OF METALS
points: The earth's crust is the major source of metals, and seawater contains soluble salts such as sodium chloride and magnesium chloride.
Naturally occurring elements or compounds in the earth's crust are minerals; minerals from which a metal can be profitably extracted are ores.

subsections.title: Extraction of Metals
points: Metals at the bottom of the activity series (gold, silver, platinum, copper) are often found free; copper and silver also occur as sulphide or oxide ores.
Metals at the top (K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al) are never found free; metals in the middle (Zn, Fe, Pb) occur mainly as oxides, sulphides or carbonates.
Metals fall into low, medium and high reactivity groups, each needing a different extraction technique (native state, reduction using carbon, electrolysis).

subsections.title: Enrichment of Ores
points: Mined ores contain impurities such as soil and sand, called gangue, which must be removed before extraction.
Separation techniques are based on differences in physical or chemical properties of gangue and ore.

subsections.title: Extracting Metals Low in the Activity Series
points: Oxides of unreactive metals can be reduced to metals by heating alone.
Cinnabar (HgS) is heated in air to mercuric oxide, which is then reduced to mercury; copper is obtained from Cu2S by heating in air.

subsections.title: Extracting Metals in the Middle of the Activity Series
points: Sulphide and carbonate ores are first converted to oxides: roasting heats sulphide ores strongly in excess air; calcination heats carbonate ores strongly in limited air.
Metal oxides are reduced using reducing agents such as carbon, e.g. ZnO + C → Zn + CO; obtaining metals from compounds is a reduction process.

Highly reactive metals like sodium, calcium and aluminium can displace less reactive metals; the highly exothermic thermit reaction of iron(III) oxide with aluminium joins railway tracks and cracked machine parts.

subsections.title: Extracting Metals towards the Top of the Activity Series
points: Carbon cannot reduce oxides of sodium, magnesium, calcium or aluminium because these metals have more affinity for oxygen than carbon.
They are obtained by electrolytic reduction of molten chlorides: metal deposits at the cathode and chlorine is liberated at the anode; aluminium is obtained from aluminium oxide.

subsections.title: Refining of Metals
points: Metals from reduction are impure; the most widely used refining method is electrolytic refining (copper, zinc, tin, nickel, silver, gold).
Impure metal is the anode, a thin strip of pure metal the cathode, and a metal salt solution the electrolyte; pure metal deposits on the cathode.
Soluble impurities go into solution and insoluble impurities settle below the anode as anode mud.

sections.title: CORROSION
points: Silver blackens by forming silver sulphide; copper gains a green coat of basic copper carbonate with moist carbon dioxide; iron in moist air gets a brown flaky coating called rust.
Iron nails rust only when exposed to both air and water, not in boiled water under oil or in dry air.

subsections.title: Prevention of Corrosion
points: Rusting can be prevented by painting, oiling, greasing, galvanising, chrome plating, anodising or making alloys.
Galvanisation coats steel and iron with a thin layer of zinc, and protects even if the zinc coating is broken.
Pure iron is soft; with about 0.05% carbon it becomes hard and strong, and with nickel and chromium it becomes stainless steel that does not rust.

An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of two or more metals, or a metal and a non-metal; an alloy with mercury is an amalgam; alloys have lower conductivity and melting point than pure metals (brass, bronze, solder).
22 carat gold is 22 parts pure gold alloyed with 2 parts copper or silver; the iron pillar near the Qutub Minar, over 1600 years old, resists rusting.

bookSummary: Elements can be classified as metals and non-metals.
Metals are lustrous, malleable, ductile and are good conductors of heat and electricity. They are solids at room temperature, except mercury which is a liquid.
Metals can form positive ions by losing electrons to non-metals.
Metals combine with oxygen to form basic oxides. Aluminium oxide and zinc oxide show the properties of both basic as well as acidic oxides. These oxides are known as amphoteric oxides.
Different metals have different reactivities with water and dilute acids.
A list of common metals arranged in order of their decreasing reactivity is known as an activity series.
Metals above hydrogen in the Activity series can displace hydrogen from dilute acids.
A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its salt solution.
Metals occur in nature as free elements or in the form of their compounds.
The extraction of metals from their ores and then refining them for use is known as metallurgy.
An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of two or more metals, or a metal and a non-metal.
The surface of some metals, such as iron, is corroded when they are exposed to moist air for a long period of time. This phenomenon is known as corrosion.
Non-metals have properties opposite to that of metals. They are neither malleable nor ductile. They are bad conductors of heat and electricity, except for graphite, which conducts electricity.
Non-metals form negatively charged ions by gaining electrons when reacting with metals.
Non-metals form oxides which are either acidic or neutral.
Non-metals do not displace hydrogen from dilute acids. They react with hydrogen to form hydrides.

chapters.title: Carbon and its Compounds
chapters.overview: The chapter explains why carbon forms covalent bonds by sharing electrons and why it forms so many compounds (catenation and tetravalency). It covers saturated and unsaturated compounds, chains, branches and rings, functional groups, homologous series and naming of carbon compounds, then their chemical properties: combustion, oxidation, addition and substitution. It describes ethanol and ethanoic acid and ends with how soaps and detergents clean.

sections.title: Carbon and its Compounds
points: Food, clothes, medicines, books and all living structures are based on carbon.
The earth's crust has only 0.02% carbon in minerals and the atmosphere has 0.03% carbon dioxide, yet carbon is immensely important.

sections.title: BONDING IN CARBON – THE COVALENT BOND
points: Most carbon compounds are poor conductors of electricity with low melting and boiling points, so the forces between molecules are weak and the bonding gives no ions.
Carbon has four valence electrons; gaining four (C4-) or losing four (C4+) would be very difficult, so carbon shares its valence electrons.
Two hydrogen atoms share electrons to form a single covalent bond in H2; oxygen atoms form a double bond in O2 and nitrogen atoms a triple bond in N2.
In methane (CH4), used as fuel and a major component of bio-gas and CNG, tetravalent carbon shares electrons with four hydrogen atoms.
Bonds formed by sharing an electron pair are covalent bonds; covalent molecules have strong bonds within but weak intermolecular forces, hence low melting and boiling points and poor conductivity.

Allotropes of carbon: in diamond each carbon bonds to four others in a rigid 3-D structure (hardest substance); in graphite each bonds to three others in hexagonal layers (smooth, slippery, good conductor); fullerenes such as C-60 are another class.

sections.title: VERSATILE NATURE OF CARBON
points: Carbon compounds with known formulae number in millions, more than those of all other elements together.
Catenation: carbon bonds with other carbon atoms giving long chains, branched chains or rings, linked by single, double or triple bonds; the carbon-carbon bond is very strong and stable.
Tetravalency: carbon bonds with four other atoms such as oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen, sulphur and chlorine; its small size makes these bonds strong.
Organic compounds were once thought to need a 'vital force', but Friedrich Wöhler prepared urea from ammonium cyanate in 1828.

subsections.title: Saturated and Unsaturated Carbon Compounds
points: Structures are drawn by linking carbon atoms with single bonds and satisfying remaining valencies with hydrogen, as for ethane (C2H6) and propane (C3H8).
Compounds in which all valencies are satisfied by single bonds are saturated and normally not very reactive.
Ethene (C2H4) needs a double bond and ethyne (C2H2) a triple bond; compounds with double or triple bonds between carbons are unsaturated and more reactive.

subsections.title: Chains, Branches and Rings
points: Chains of carbon give methane, ethane, propane, butane, pentane and hexane.
Butane (C4H10) has two possible carbon skeletons; compounds with identical molecular formula but different structures are structural isomers.
Some compounds have rings, e.g. cyclohexane (C6H12) and benzene (C6H6).
Compounds of only carbon and hydrogen are hydrocarbons: saturated ones are alkanes, those with double bonds alkenes, and those with triple bonds alkynes.

subsections.title: Will you be my Friend?
points: Hydrogen in a hydrocarbon chain can be replaced by halogens, oxygen, nitrogen or sulphur; the replacing element is a heteroatom.
Heteroatoms and groups containing them confer specific properties regardless of chain length and are called functional groups: halo (-Cl, -Br), alcohol (-OH), aldehyde, ketone and carboxylic acid.

subsections.title: Homologous Series
points: A series of compounds in which the same functional group substitutes for hydrogen in a carbon chain is a homologous series, e.g. CH3OH, C2H5OH, C3H7OH, C4H9OH.
Successive members differ by a -CH2- unit; the general formula for alkenes is CnH2n.
Physical properties such as melting and boiling points and solubility show gradation with increasing molecular mass, while chemical properties, determined by the functional group, remain similar.

subsections.title: Nomenclature of Carbon Compounds
points: Names are based on the basic carbon chain modified by a prefix or suffix for the functional group.
Identify the number of carbon atoms (three carbons: propane) and show the functional group as a prefix or suffix.
If the suffix begins with a vowel, delete the final 'e' of the chain name, e.g. propane - e + one = propanone.
For unsaturated chains, 'ane' is replaced by 'ene' or 'yne', e.g. propene, propyne; examples: chloropropane, propanol, propanal, propanoic acid.

sections.title: CHEMICAL PROPERTIES OF CARBON COMPOUNDS
points: Since most fuels are carbon or its compounds, combustion is studied first, followed by oxidation, addition and substitution reactions.

subsections.title: Combustion
points: Carbon in all allotropic forms burns in oxygen to give carbon dioxide with heat and light; most carbon compounds also release much heat and light.
Saturated hydrocarbons generally give a clean flame, unsaturated compounds a yellow sooty flame; limited air causes incomplete combustion and a sooty flame.
Blackened vessel bottoms mean blocked air holes and wasted fuel; burning coal and petroleum forms oxides of sulphur and nitrogen, major pollutants.
A flame is produced only when gaseous substances burn; coal and petroleum formed from biomass over millions of years and are fossil fuels.

subsections.title: Oxidation
points: Besides complete oxidation on combustion, alcohols can be converted to carboxylic acids.
Alkaline potassium permanganate and acidified potassium dichromate add oxygen to alcohols and are oxidising agents.

subsections.title: Addition Reaction
points: Unsaturated hydrocarbons add hydrogen in the presence of catalysts such as palladium or nickel to give saturated hydrocarbons.
Catalysts cause a reaction to occur or proceed at a different rate without being affected; hydrogenation of vegetable oils uses a nickel catalyst.
Vegetable oils have long unsaturated chains and animal fats saturated chains; oils with unsaturated fatty acids should be chosen for cooking.

subsections.title: Substitution Reaction
points: Saturated hydrocarbons are fairly unreactive, but in sunlight chlorine replaces hydrogen atoms one by one in a very fast reaction.
One type of atom or group taking the place of another is a substitution reaction, e.g. CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl.

sections.title: SOME IMPORTANT CARBON COMPOUNDS – ETHANOL AND ETHANOIC ACID
points: Ethanol and ethanoic acid are two commercially important carbon compounds.

subsections.title: Properties of Ethanol
points: Ethanol (alcohol) is a liquid, the active ingredient of alcoholic drinks, a good solvent used in tincture iodine, cough syrups and tonics, and soluble in water in all proportions.
Even a small quantity of pure ethanol (absolute alcohol) can be lethal, and long-term consumption causes health problems; methanol in very small quantities can cause death or blindness.
Ethanol reacts with sodium to evolve hydrogen and form sodium ethoxide.
Heating ethanol at 443 K with excess concentrated sulphuric acid dehydrates it to ethene; the acid is a dehydrating agent.
Industrial ethanol mixed with methanol and blue dye is denatured alcohol; ethanol from sugarcane molasses is used as a cleaner fuel additive in petrol.

subsections.title: Properties of Ethanoic Acid
points: Ethanoic acid (acetic acid) is a carboxylic acid; a 5-8% solution is vinegar, and pure acid melting at 290 K freezes in winter, hence glacial acetic acid.
Carboxylic acids are weak acids, unlike completely ionised mineral acids such as HCl.

Esterification: ethanoic acid and absolute ethanol with an acid catalyst give a sweet-smelling ester used in perfumes and flavouring; NaOH converts the ester back to alcohol and a sodium salt (saponification).
Ethanoic acid reacts with sodium hydroxide to give sodium acetate and water, and with carbonates and hydrogencarbonates to give salt, carbon dioxide and water.

sections.title: SOAPS AND DETERGENTS
points: Soap molecules are sodium or potassium salts of long-chain carboxylic acids; the ionic end interacts with water and the carbon chain with oil.
Soap molecules form micelles with hydrophobic tails inside around oily dirt and ionic ends outside, forming an emulsion so dirt is rinsed away; micelles scatter light, making soap solution cloudy.
In hard water, soap reacts with calcium and magnesium salts to form scum, so more soap is needed.

Detergents, sodium salts of sulphonic acids or ammonium salts with chloride or bromide ions, do not form insoluble precipitates with calcium and magnesium ions and remain effective in hard water; they are used in shampoos and cleaning products.

bookSummary: Carbon is a versatile element that forms the basis for all living organisms and many of the things we use.
This large variety of compounds is formed by carbon because of its tetravalency and the property of catenation that it exhibits.
Covalent bonds are formed by the sharing of electrons between two atoms so that both can achieve a completely filled outermost shell.
Carbon forms covalent bonds with itself and other elements such as hydrogen, oxygen, sulphur, nitrogen and chlorine.
Carbon also forms compounds containing double and triple bonds between carbon atoms. These carbon chains may be in the form of straight chains, branched chains or rings.
The ability of carbon to form chains gives rise to a homologous series of compounds in which the same functional group is attached to carbon chains of different lengths.
The functional groups such as alcohols, aldehydes, ketones and carboxylic acids bestow characteristic properties to the carbon compounds that contain them.
Carbon and its compounds are some of our major sources of fuels.
Ethanol and ethanoic acid are carbon compounds of importance in our daily lives.
The action of soaps and detergents is based on the presence of both hydrophobic and hydrophilic groups in the molecule and this helps to emulsify the oily dirt and hence its removal.

chapters.title: Life Processes
chapters.overview: The chapter explains that living organisms must continuously maintain their ordered structures, and that the processes doing this - nutrition, respiration, transportation and excretion - are life processes. It describes autotrophic nutrition (photosynthesis) and heterotrophic nutrition, including digestion in human beings; aerobic and anaerobic respiration and breathing in humans; transport by the heart, blood vessels, platelets and lymph in humans and by xylem and phloem in plants; and excretion by nephrons in humans and by various strategies in plants.

sections.title: Life Processes
points: Visible movement is not enough to define life, since plants not visibly growing and animals breathing without visible movement are still alive.
Biologists consider invisible molecular movement necessary for life; viruses show none until they infect a cell, which is partly why their status as living is controversial.
Living structures are organised and tend to break down, so organisms must keep repairing and maintaining them by moving molecules around.

sections.title: WHAT ARE LIFE PROCESSES?
points: The processes which together perform the maintenance job of living organisms are life processes.
Energy from outside the body, food, is brought in by nutrition; oxygen acquired and used to break down food for cellular needs is respiration.
In multi-cellular organisms not all cells touch the environment, so simple diffusion is insufficient and a transportation system is needed.
Harmful by-products of energy generation are removed from the body by excretion.

sections.title: NUTRITION
points: Food is the source of energy and materials for growth, development and synthesis of proteins.
Autotrophs (green plants and some bacteria) use simple inorganic materials, carbon dioxide and water.
Heterotrophs (animals and fungi) use complex substances broken down by bio-catalysts called enzymes, and depend directly or indirectly on autotrophs.

subsections.title: Autotrophic Nutrition
points: Photosynthesis converts carbon dioxide and water into carbohydrates in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll; unused carbohydrates are stored as starch (humans store energy as glycogen).

Events of photosynthesis: absorption of light by chlorophyll; conversion of light to chemical energy and splitting of water into hydrogen and oxygen; reduction of carbon dioxide to carbohydrates. Desert plants take up CO2 at night.
Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll; a variegated leaf starch test shows chlorophyll is essential, and a potassium hydroxide set-up shows carbon dioxide is needed.
Stomata are tiny pores on leaves for gaseous exchange; guard cells swell with water to open the pore and shrink to close it, limiting water loss.
Water, nitrogen, phosphorus, iron and magnesium come from the soil; nitrogen is taken up as nitrates or nitrites or as organic compounds prepared by bacteria.

subsections.title: Heterotrophic Nutrition
points: The form of nutrition depends on the type and availability of food and how it is obtained, e.g. a stationary food source (grass) versus a mobile one (deer).
Fungi such as bread moulds, yeast and mushrooms break food down outside the body and absorb it; others take in whole material and break it down inside.
Parasites such as cuscuta (amar-bel), ticks, lice, leeches and tape-worms derive nutrition from plants or animals without killing them.

subsections.title: How do Organisms obtain their Nutrition?
points: In single-celled organisms food may be taken in by the entire surface.
Amoeba uses temporary finger-like extensions to enclose food in a food-vacuole, where it is broken down and diffuses into the cytoplasm; undigested material is thrown out.
Paramoecium has a definite shape and takes in food at a specific spot, moved there by cilia.

subsections.title: Nutrition in Human Beings
points: The alimentary canal is a long tube from mouth to anus; teeth crush food, and saliva from salivary glands contains salivary amylase that breaks starch into simple sugar.
Rhythmic peristaltic movements push food along the gut; the oesophagus carries food to the stomach, whose gastric glands release hydrochloric acid, pepsin and mucus.
A sphincter releases food into the small intestine, the longest part and site of complete digestion of carbohydrates, proteins and fats; herbivores have a longer small intestine than carnivores.

Bile from the liver makes food alkaline and emulsifies fats; pancreatic juice contains trypsin and lipase; intestinal juice converts proteins to amino acids, carbohydrates to glucose and fats to fatty acids and glycerol.
Villi increase the surface area for absorption and carry food to cells via blood; the large intestine absorbs water and the anal sphincter regulates exit of waste.
Dental caries begins when bacteria acting on sugars produce acids that demineralise enamel; brushing removes plaque.

sections.title: RESPIRATION
points: Exhaled air turns lime water milky faster than ordinary air; yeast fermenting sugar also produces carbon dioxide.
Glucose is first broken into three-carbon pyruvate in the cytoplasm; in yeast pyruvate becomes ethanol and carbon dioxide without oxygen (anaerobic respiration).
In mitochondria pyruvate is broken down with oxygen into carbon dioxide and water (aerobic respiration), releasing much more energy; lack of oxygen in muscles gives lactic acid, causing cramps.
Energy from respiration is used to make ATP, the energy currency of the cell; breaking the terminal phosphate linkage releases 30.5 kJ/mol.
Plants exchange gases by diffusion through stomata and intercellular spaces; at night CO2 elimination dominates and in the day oxygen release does.
Aquatic animals breathe much faster because dissolved oxygen is low; fishes pass water over gills.

In humans air passes through nostrils (filtered by hairs and mucus), throat (with rings of cartilage) and lungs to alveoli, where blood exchanges gases; breathing in lifts ribs and flattens the diaphragm; lungs always hold a residual volume of air.

Haemoglobin in red blood corpuscles carries oxygen, while carbon dioxide is mostly transported dissolved in blood; the alveolar surface would cover about 80 m2. Tobacco and smoking harm health and cause cancers.

sections.title: TRANSPORTATION
points: Blood transports food, oxygen and waste materials, requiring a pump, a network of tubes and a repair system.

subsections.title: Transportation in Human Beings
points: Blood is a fluid connective tissue: plasma carries food, carbon dioxide and nitrogenous wastes dissolved, and red blood corpuscles carry oxygen.

Our pump - the heart: a muscular organ with four chambers; oxygen-rich blood from the lungs enters the left atrium, passes to the left ventricle and is pumped to the body; de-oxygenated blood enters the right atrium, passes to the right ventricle and is pumped to the lungs; valves prevent backflow.

Separating the two sides supports birds and mammals with high energy needs; amphibians and many reptiles have three-chambered hearts, fishes two chambers; blood passing twice through the heart per cycle is double circulation.

Blood pressure is the force blood exerts against a vessel wall; normal systolic pressure is about 120 mm Hg and diastolic 80 mm Hg, measured with a sphygmomanometer; high blood pressure is hypertension.
The tubes - blood vessels: arteries carry blood away from the heart with thick elastic walls; veins bring blood back and have valves; capillaries one cell thick allow exchange with cells.

Maintenance by platelets: platelets plug leaks by helping blood clot at injuries; lymph (tissue fluid), colourless with less protein than plasma, carries absorbed fat from the intestine and drains excess fluid back into blood.

subsections.title: Transportation in Plants
points: Roots absorb raw materials from soil; over large distances diffusion is not enough, but plants have low energy needs and can use slow transport systems.
Xylem moves water and minerals from the soil; phloem transports products of photosynthesis from leaves to other parts.

Transport of water: root cells actively take up ions, so water moves in and is pushed up; evaporation of water from leaves (transpiration) creates a suction pulling water up, and also helps temperature regulation. Root pressure matters more at night and transpiration pull during the day.
Transport of food and other substances: translocation of soluble photosynthetic products, amino acids and other substances occurs in phloem sieve tubes with companion cells, upward and downward.
Translocation uses energy from ATP to load sucrose into phloem, raising osmotic pressure so material moves to tissues with less pressure, e.g. stored sugar to buds in spring.

sections.title: EXCRETION
points: Excretion is the biological process of removing harmful metabolic wastes, such as nitrogenous materials, from the body.
Many unicellular organisms remove wastes by simple diffusion into surrounding water; complex multi-cellular organisms use specialised organs.

subsections.title: Excretion in Human Beings
points: The excretory system has a pair of kidneys, a pair of ureters, a urinary bladder and a urethra.
Nitrogenous wastes such as urea or uric acid are filtered from blood in nephrons, where capillary clusters sit in the cup-shaped Bowman's capsule.
Glucose, amino acids, salts and much water are selectively re-absorbed; the amount of water re-absorbed depends on excess water and dissolved waste.
Urine is stored in the muscular bladder, under nervous control, until passed out through the urethra.
An artificial kidney removes nitrogenous wastes by dialysis through semi-permeable tubes, without re-absorption; the daily initial filtrate of about 180 L gives only a litre or two of urine.

subsections.title: Excretion in Plants
points: Oxygen from photosynthesis can be thought of as a waste; excess water is lost by transpiration.
Wastes are stored in cell vacuoles, in leaves that fall off, or as resins and gums especially in old xylem, and some are excreted into the soil.
Organ donation: organs such as corneas, kidneys, heart, liver and bone marrow can be donated with consent to save or transform a recipient's life.

keyResults.label: Alveolar surface
keyResults.statement: If spread out, the alveolar surface would cover about 80 m2; diffusion alone would take about 3 years to move oxygen from lungs to toes.

keyResults.label: Kidney filtrate
keyResults.statement: The initial filtrate in the kidneys of a healthy adult is about 180 L daily, but only a litre or two is excreted.

keyResults.label: Digestion end products
keyResults.statement: Intestinal juice enzymes convert proteins to amino acids, complex carbohydrates into glucose and fats into fatty acids and glycerol.

bookSummary: Movement of various types can be taken as an indication of life.
Maintenance of life requires processes like nutrition, respiration, transport of materials within the body and excretion of waste products.
Autotrophic nutrition involves the intake of simple inorganic materials from the environment and using an external energy source like the Sun to synthesise complex high-energy organic material.
Heterotrophic nutrition involves the intake of complex material prepared by other organisms.
In human beings, the food eaten is broken down by various steps along the alimentary canal and the digested food is absorbed in the small intestine to be sent to all cells in the body.
During the process of respiration, organic compounds such as glucose are broken down to provide energy in the form of ATP. ATP is used to provide energy for other reactions in the cell.
Respiration may be aerobic or anaerobic. Aerobic respiration makes more energy available to the organism.

In human beings, the transport of materials such as oxygen, carbon dioxide, food and excretory products is a function of the circulatory system. The circulatory system consists of the heart, blood and blood vessels.
In highly differentiated plants, transport of water, minerals, food and other materials is a function of the vascular tissue which consists of xylem and phloem.
In human beings, excretory products in the form of soluble nitrogen compounds are removed by the nephrons in the kidneys.

Plants use a variety of techniques to get rid of waste material. For example, waste material may be stored in the cell-vacuoles or as gum and resin, removed in the falling leaves, or excreted into the surrounding soil.

chapters.title: Control and Coordination
chapters.overview: The chapter explains that living organisms respond to changes in their environment with carefully controlled movements, using systems for control and coordination. In animals this is done by the nervous system (neurons, reflex arcs, the brain and spinal cord, and muscles) and by hormones of the endocrine system; plants, having no nervous system, respond by immediate movements or growth movements coordinated by plant hormones. It describes important animal hormones and their feedback regulation.

sections.title: Control and Coordination
points: Some movements result from growth, as in a germinating seedling, while others, like a cat running, are not connected with growth.
Movement is a response to a change in the environment, used to the organism's advantage, and each change evokes an appropriate, controlled movement.
Multicellular organisms use specialised tissues to provide control and coordination.

sections.title: ANIMALS – NERVOUS SYSTEM
points: In animals, control and coordination are provided by nervous and muscular tissues.
Receptors at specialised tips of nerve cells, located in sense organs, detect information; gustatory receptors detect taste and olfactory receptors smell.
Information at the dendritic tip sets off a chemical reaction creating an electrical impulse that travels from dendrite to cell body and along the axon.
At the axon end, chemicals are released that cross the gap (synapse) and start an impulse in the next neuron, or reach muscle cells or glands.
Nervous tissue is an organised network of neurons specialised for conducting information by electrical impulses.

subsections.title: What happens in Reflex Actions?
points: A reflex is doing something without thinking about it, such as pulling the hand back from a flame.
Thinking through the brain, at the forward end of the skull, may take too long in an emergency.
A simpler connection between nerves detecting input and nerves moving muscles is a reflex arc; reflex arcs form in the spinal cord, though the input also reaches the brain.
Reflex arcs evolved because the brain's thinking is not fast enough, and remain more efficient for quick responses.

subsections.title: Human Brain
points: The brain and spinal cord constitute the central nervous system; the brain is the main coordinating centre.
Voluntary actions such as writing and talking are based on deciding what to do next; the peripheral nervous system of cranial and spinal nerves links the central nervous system with the body.
The brain has three main regions: fore-brain, mid-brain and hind-brain.
The fore-brain is the main thinking part, with sensory areas, association areas and motor areas controlling voluntary muscles, and a centre associated with hunger.

Involuntary actions are controlled by the mid-brain and hind-brain; the medulla controls blood pressure, salivation and vomiting, and the cerebellum is responsible for precision of voluntary actions and posture and balance.

subsections.title: How are these Tissues protected?
points: The brain sits inside a bony box and is contained in a fluid-filled balloon that absorbs shocks.
The vertebral column or backbone protects the spinal cord.

subsections.title: How does the Nervous Tissue cause Action?
points: Muscle tissue does the final job of action when a nerve impulse reaches it.
Muscle cells move by changing shape to shorten; special proteins change their shape and arrangement in response to nervous electrical impulses.
There are different kinds of muscles, such as voluntary and involuntary muscles.

sections.title: COORDINATION IN PLANTS
points: Plants have neither a nervous system nor muscles but still respond to stimuli.
Leaves of the chhui-mui (sensitive plant) fold on touch without growth, while the directional movement of a seedling is caused by growth.
Plants show two types of movement: one dependent on growth and one independent of growth.

subsections.title: Immediate Response to Stimulus
points: In the sensitive plant, movement happens at a point different from the point of touch, so information must be communicated.
Plants use electrical-chemical means to convey information from cell to cell, but have no specialised conducting tissue.
Plant cells change shape by changing the amount of water in them, swelling or shrinking.

subsections.title: Movement Due to Growth
points: Pea plant tendrils are sensitive to touch; the part in contact with a support grows less rapidly than the part away from it, so the tendril circles the object.
Directional or tropic movements can be towards or away from a stimulus: shoots bend towards light and roots away from it (phototropism).
Roots grow downwards and shoots upwards in response to gravity (geotropism); growth of pollen tubes towards ovules is chemotropism; hydrotropism relates to water.

Electrical impulses reach only cells connected by nervous tissue and cells need time to reset, so most multicellular organisms also use chemical communication by hormones, which is slower but reaches all cells.

Auxin, made at the shoot tip, diffuses to the shady side and makes cells there grow longer, so the shoot bends towards light; gibberellins help stem growth, cytokinins promote cell division, and abscisic acid inhibits growth and causes wilting of leaves.

sections.title: HORMONES IN ANIMALS
points: In a scary situation, adrenaline from the adrenal glands is secreted directly into the blood; the heart beats faster, blood is diverted from the digestive system and skin to skeletal muscles, and breathing rate increases.
Animal hormones are part of the endocrine system, a second way of control and coordination.
Iodine is needed for the thyroid gland to make thyroxin, which regulates carbohydrate, protein and fat metabolism; iodine deficiency may cause goitre, with a swollen neck.
Growth hormone from the pituitary regulates growth; its deficiency in childhood leads to dwarfism. Testosterone in males and oestrogen in females cause changes at puberty.
Insulin from the pancreas regulates blood sugar; if not secreted properly, blood sugar rises (diabetes). The hypothalamus releases growth hormone releasing factor to stimulate the pituitary.
The timing and amount of hormones released are regulated by feedback mechanisms, e.g. rising blood sugar makes the pancreas produce more insulin.

bookSummary: Control and coordination are the functions of the nervous system and hormones in our bodies.
The responses of the nervous system can be classified as reflex action, voluntary action or involuntary action.
The nervous system uses electrical impulses to transmit messages.
The nervous system gets information from our sense organs and acts through our muscles.
Chemical coordination is seen in both plants and animals.
Hormones produced in one part of an organism move to another part to achieve the desired effect.
A feedback mechanism regulates the action of the hormones.

chapters.title: How do Organisms Reproduce?
chapters.overview: The chapter explains that reproduction involves copying DNA along with cellular apparatus, and that inbuilt variation in copying is important for the survival of species. It describes asexual modes used by single organisms - fission, fragmentation, regeneration, budding, vegetative propagation and spore formation - and then sexual reproduction: why it generates more variation, reproduction in flowering plants, and human reproduction including puberty, the male and female reproductive systems, menstruation and reproductive health.

sections.title: How do Organisms Reproduce?
points: Reproduction is not necessary to maintain the life of an individual, and it costs energy.
We notice organisms because they reproduce, and reproducing organisms create new individuals that look very much like themselves.

sections.title: DO ORGANISMS CREATE EXACT COPIES OF THEMSELVES?
points: Chromosomes in the nucleus carry information for inheritance as DNA, the information source for making proteins; changed information leads to altered body designs.
A basic event in reproduction is creating a DNA copy, accompanied by creation of additional cellular apparatus, after which the cell divides into two.
No bio-chemical reaction is absolutely reliable, so DNA copies are similar but may not be identical; drastic variations kill the new cell, others survive.
This inbuilt tendency for variation during reproduction is the basis for evolution.

subsections.title: The Importance of Variation
points: Populations fill well-defined niches, and consistent DNA copying maintains body designs suited to the niche, linking reproduction to population stability.
Niches can change drastically (temperature, water levels, meteorite hits) and could wipe out a population.
Variants may survive such changes, e.g. heat-resistant bacteria surviving warming waters, so variation is useful for the survival of species over time.

sections.title: MODES OF REPRODUCTION USED BY SINGLE ORGANISMS
points: The modes by which organisms reproduce depend on their body design.
Yeast grown in sugar solution and mould on moist bread are observed to compare how they grow.

subsections.title: Fission
points: In unicellular organisms, cell division or fission creates new individuals; many bacteria and protozoa split into two equal halves.
In Amoeba splitting can take place in any plane, while Leishmania (which causes kala-azar), with a whip-like structure, divides in a definite orientation.
Plasmodium, the malarial parasite, divides into many daughter cells simultaneously by multiple fission; yeast puts out small buds.

subsections.title: Fragmentation
points: Spirogyra simply breaks up into smaller pieces on maturation, and the fragments grow into new individuals.
Most multi-cellular organisms, with cells organised into tissues and organs at definite positions, cannot divide cell-by-cell and need more complex ways of reproduction.
Reproduction in such organisms is the function of a specific cell type capable of growing, proliferating and making other cell types.

subsections.title: Regeneration
points: Hydra and Planaria can be cut into pieces and each piece grows into a complete organism; this is regeneration.
Specialised cells proliferate and change into various cell types and tissues in an organised sequence called development.
Regeneration is not the same as reproduction, since most organisms do not depend on being cut up to reproduce.

subsections.title: Budding
points: Hydra uses regenerative cells for reproduction by budding.
A bud develops as an outgrowth from repeated cell division at one site, grows into a tiny individual and detaches when mature.

subsections.title: Vegetative Propagation
points: In many plants, roots, stems and leaves develop into new plants; layering and grafting are used for sugarcane, roses and grapes.
Such plants flower and fruit earlier than seed-grown ones, allow propagation of seedless plants like banana, orange, rose and jasmine, and are genetically similar to the parent.
Buds in notches along Bryophyllum leaf margins fall on soil and grow into new plants.
In tissue culture, cells from a growing tip are grown in an artificial medium into a callus, then in a hormone medium into plantlets, giving many disease-free plants from one parent.

subsections.title: Spore Formation
points: Threads on bread mould (Rhizopus) are hyphae; the blob-on-a-stick structures are sporangia containing spores that develop into new individuals.
Spores have thick protective walls until they reach a moist surface and grow.
Modes creating new generations from a single individual are asexual reproduction.

sections.title: SEXUAL REPRODUCTION
points: Some modes of reproduction need both sexes, males and females, to produce new generations, as with bulls and hens.

subsections.title: Why the Sexual Mode of Reproduction?
points: DNA copying errors create variation useful for species survival, but copying is precise enough that variation arises slowly.
Combining accumulated variations from two individuals creates novel combinations; sexual reproduction combines DNA from two individuals.
To avoid doubling DNA each generation, germ-cells with half the chromosomes and DNA are made by meiosis, and fusion restores the number.
In complex organisms the germ-cells specialise: the motile one is the male gamete and the one with stored food is the female gamete.

subsections.title: Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
points: Stamens and pistil in the flower are the reproductive parts; flowers are unisexual (papaya, watermelon) or bisexual (Hibiscus, mustard).
The stamen produces pollen grains; the pistil has an ovary with ovules containing egg cells, a style and a stigma.
Transfer of pollen in the same flower is self-pollination and between flowers cross-pollination, by wind, water or animals; a pollen tube grows through the style to the ovary.
Fusion of germ-cells (fertilisation) gives a zygote that forms an embryo; the ovule becomes a seed and the ovary a fruit, and the seed's embryo develops into a seedling by germination.

subsections.title: Reproduction in Human Beings
points: In early teens, changes common to boys and girls include thick hair in armpits and genital area, oily skin and pimples.
Girls show increased breast size and begin to menstruate; boys develop facial hair and their voices crack; changes happen gradually and differ between people.
As general body growth slows, reproductive tissues mature; this period during adolescence is puberty.
Changes at puberty signal sexual maturity, and special organs are needed for transfer of germ-cells; female organs and breasts mature to carry and feed a baby.

subsections.title: Male Reproductive System
points: Sperms form in the testes, located outside the abdominal cavity in the scrotum because sperm formation needs a lower temperature.
Testosterone regulates sperm formation and brings about changes in boys at puberty.

Sperms pass through the vas deferens, which joins a tube from the bladder, so the urethra is a common passage for sperms and urine; the prostate and seminal vesicles add fluid for transport and nutrition.
Sperms consist mainly of genetic material with a long tail for movement.

subsections.title: Female Reproductive System
points: Eggs are made in the ovaries, which also produce hormones; at birth the ovaries hold thousands of immature eggs, and from puberty one egg is produced each month.
The egg travels through the oviduct (fallopian tube) to the uterus, which opens into the vagina through the cervix; fertilisation occurs in the oviduct.

The embryo implants in the thickened uterine lining and develops into a foetus, nourished through the placenta, whose villi provide a large surface for glucose and oxygen to pass and wastes to be removed.
Development takes about nine months, and the child is born by rhythmic contractions of uterine muscles.

subsections.title: What happens when the Egg is not Fertilised?
points: An unfertilised egg lives for about one day.
The thick, spongy uterine lining prepared each month is not needed and breaks down, coming out through the vagina as blood and mucous.
This monthly cycle is menstruation and usually lasts about two to eight days.

subsections.title: Reproductive Health
points: Some sexual maturation does not mean the body or mind is ready for sexual acts or bringing up children, and there are pressures from friends, family and government.
Sexually transmitted diseases include gonorrhoea and syphilis (bacterial) and warts and HIV-AIDS (viral); condoms help prevent transmission to some extent.

Contraceptive methods include mechanical barriers (condoms), hormonal oral pills, devices like the loop or copper-T in the uterus, and surgical blocking of the vas deferens or fallopian tube, each with possible side effects.
Illegal sex-selective abortion of female foetuses is lowering the child sex ratio, though prenatal sex determination is prohibited by law.
Population size depends on birth and death rates; inequality may matter more than population size for poor living standards.

Growing new plants from tissue or cells of a growing tip in an artificial medium.

Blob-like structures in Rhizopus containing spores that develop into new individuals.
Modes of reproduction in which new generations are created from a single individual.

The motile germ-cell and the germ-cell containing stored food, respectively.

The roughly monthly breakdown and discharge of the uterine lining as blood and mucous when the egg is not fertilised.
Ways devised to avoid pregnancy: mechanical barriers, hormonal pills, devices such as copper-T, and surgical methods.

keyResults.label: Basic event of reproduction
keyResults.statement: Creation of a DNA copy together with additional cellular apparatus, followed by division of the cell.

keyResults.label: Menstruation
keyResults.statement: An unfertilised egg lives about one day; menstruation occurs roughly every month and usually lasts about two to eight days.

keyResults.label: Human pregnancy
keyResults.statement: The development of the child inside the mother's body takes approximately nine months.

keyResults.label: Fertilisation site
keyResults.statement: Fertilisation in human beings occurs in the fallopian tube (oviduct).

bookSummary: Reproduction, unlike other life processes, is not essential to maintain the life of an individual organism.
Reproduction involves creation of a DNA copy and additional cellular apparatus by the cell involved in the process.
Various organisms use different modes of reproduction depending on their body design.
In fission, many bacteria and protozoa simply divide into two or more daughter cells.
Organisms such as hydra can regenerate if they are broken into pieces. They can also give out buds which mature into new individuals.
Roots, stems and leaves of some plants develop into new plants through vegetative propagation.
These are examples of asexual reproduction where new generations are created from a single individual.
Sexual reproduction involves two individuals for the creation of a new individual.
DNA copying mechanisms creates variations which are useful for ensuring the survival of the species. Modes of sexual reproduction allow for greater variation to be generated.
Reproduction in flowering plants involves transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma which is referred to as pollination. This is followed by fertilisation.
Changes in the body at puberty, such as increase in breast size in girls and new facial hair growth in boys, are signs of sexual maturation.
The male reproductive system in human beings consists of testes which produce sperms, vas deferens, seminal vesicles, prostate gland, urethra and penis.
The female reproductive system in human beings consists of ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus and vagina.
Sexual reproduction in human beings involves the introduction of sperm in the vagina of the female. Fertilisation occurs in the fallopian tube.
Contraception to avoid pregnancy can be achieved by the use of condoms, oral pills, copper-T and other methods.

chapters.title: Heredity
chapters.overview: The chapter studies how variations are created and inherited. It shows how variation accumulates over generations, more so with sexual reproduction, then describes inherited traits and Mendel's experiments with garden peas, which revealed dominant and recessive traits and independent inheritance. It explains how genes control traits through proteins, how chromosomes carry gene sets, and how sex is determined in human beings by X and Y chromosomes.

sections.title: Heredity
points: Reproduction gives rise to individuals that are similar but subtly different; sexual reproduction maximises successful variations.
A field of sugarcane shows little variation, while sexually reproducing animals including humans show distinct variations.

sections.title: ACCUMULATION OF VARIATION DURING REPRODUCTION
points: Inheritance provides a common basic body design and subtle changes; each generation has inherited differences plus newly created ones.
In asexual reproduction, such as bacteria dividing, individuals are very similar, differing only through small inaccuracies in DNA copying; sexual reproduction generates greater diversity.
Variations do not have equal chances of survival; e.g. heat-resistant bacteria survive a heat wave better.
Selection of variants by environmental factors forms the basis for evolutionary processes.

sections.title: HEREDITY
points: The rules of heredity determine the process by which traits and characteristics are reliably inherited.

subsections.title: Inherited Traits
points: A child bears all the basic features of a human being but does not look exactly like its parents, and human populations show much variation.
Free and attached earlobes are two variants found in human populations, used to suggest a rule of inheritance.

subsections.title: Rules for the Inheritance of Traits – Mendel’s Contributions
points: Father and mother contribute practically equal genetic material, so each trait has two versions in each child.
Mendel crossed garden peas with contrasting characters (round/wrinkled seeds, tall/short plants, white/violet flowers); a tall × short cross gave all tall F1 plants, with no medium-height plants.
Self-pollinated F1 tall plants gave F2 progeny of which one quarter were short, so both traits were inherited but only tallness was expressed.
Mendel proposed two copies of factors (now called genes) control traits; TT and Tt are tall and only tt is short, so 'T' is dominant and 't' recessive, with F2 in a 1:2:1 ratio of TT, Tt and tt.

Crossing tall round-seeded with short wrinkled-seeded plants gave F2 with new combinations, showing traits are independently inherited; a round-yellow × wrinkled-green cross gave F2 in a 9:3:3:1 ratio.
Gregor Johann Mendel (1822-1884), educated in a monastery and at the University of Vienna, was the first to keep count of individuals showing a trait in each generation.

subsections.title: How do these Traits get Expressed?
points: A section of DNA that provides information for one protein is the gene for that protein.
Plant height may depend on the amount of a growth hormone, which depends on the efficiency of an enzyme; an altered, less efficient enzyme gene gives a short plant. Thus genes control traits.
Each pea plant has two sets of genes, one from each parent, and each germ cell has only one gene set.

Gene sets are present as separate pieces called chromosomes; each cell has two copies of each chromosome and each germ cell takes one from each pair, restoring the number on fusion and explaining independent inheritance.

subsections.title: Sex Determination
points: Some species rely on environmental cues: in a few reptiles the temperature of fertilised eggs decides sex, and snails can change sex.
In human beings sex is largely genetically determined; humans have 22 paired chromosomes plus a pair of sex chromosomes.
Women have a perfect pair, XX; men have a mismatched pair, XY, with a short Y chromosome.
All children inherit an X from the mother; a child inheriting X from the father is a girl and one inheriting Y is a boy, so half the children are boys and half girls.

keyTerms.meaning: The process, following rules, by which traits and characteristics are reliably inherited.
Differences between individuals, inherited from previous generations or newly created during reproduction.
First-generation and second-generation progeny in Mendel's crosses.
Factors, two copies of which control traits; a section of DNA that provides information for one protein.
A trait like 'T' of which a single copy is enough to be expressed.
A trait like 't' that is expressed only when both copies are of that kind.
Each of the separate independent pieces of DNA in which a gene set is present.
The pair of human chromosomes, X and Y, that is not always a perfect pair; women are XX and men XY.

keyResults.label: Monohybrid cross
keyResults.statement: Tall (TT) × short (tt) gives all tall F1 (Tt); F1 self-pollinated gives F2 with one quarter short, in the ratio 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt.

keyResults.label: Dihybrid cross (Fig. 8.5)
keyResults.statement: RRyy (round, green) × rrYY (wrinkled, yellow) gives F1 RrYy (round, yellow); F2 of 556 seeds: 315 round yellow, 108 round green, 101 wrinkled yellow, 32 wrinkled green, a 9:3:3:1 ratio.

keyResults.label: Independent inheritance
keyResults.statement: The tall/short trait and the round seed/wrinkled seed trait are independently inherited.

keyResults.label: Human chromosomes
keyResults.statement: Humans have 22 pairs of chromosomes with maternal and paternal copies plus one pair of sex chromosomes: XX in women, XY in men.

keyResults.label: Sex determination in humans
keyResults.statement: The sex of the child depends on whether the paternal chromosome is X (for girls) or Y (for boys).

keyResults.label: Gregor Johann Mendel
keyResults.statement: 1822-1884; worked out the main rules of inheritance using garden peas.

bookSummary: Variations arising during the process of reproduction can be inherited.
These variations may lead to increased survival of the individuals.

Sexually reproducing individuals have two copies of genes for the same trait. If the copies are not identical, the trait that gets expressed is called the dominant trait and the other is called the recessive trait.
Traits in one individual may be inherited separately, giving rise to new combinations of traits in the offspring of sexual reproduction.
Sex is determined by different factors in various species. In human beings, the sex of the child depends on whether the paternal chromosome is X (for girls) or Y (for boys).
