chapters.title: Light – Reflection and Refraction
chapters.overview: The chapter studies reflection and refraction of light using its straight-line propagation. It covers the laws of reflection, spherical mirrors and their terms, image formation and ray diagrams for concave and convex mirrors, the New Cartesian Sign Convention, the mirror formula and magnification. It then covers refraction through a glass slab, the laws of refraction and refractive index, spherical lenses, image formation and ray diagrams for lenses, the lens formula, magnification and power of a lens, with worked examples.

sections.title: Light – Reflection and Refraction
points: An object reflects light falling on it, and this reflected light received by our eyes enables us to see; light is transmitted through transparent media.
A small source casting a sharp shadow of an opaque object shows light travels in straight lines, indicated as a ray of light.
When an obstacle is very small light bends around it (diffraction), explained by treating light as a wave; modern quantum theory reconciles its wave and particle properties.

sections.title: REFLECTION OF LIGHT
points: A highly polished surface such as a mirror reflects most of the light falling on it.

Laws of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection; the incident ray, the normal at the point of incidence and the reflected ray lie in the same plane. They apply to all reflecting surfaces including spherical ones.
A plane mirror image is always virtual and erect, the same size as the object, as far behind the mirror as the object is in front, and laterally inverted.
Mirrors whose reflecting surfaces are spherical, like the curved surface of a shining spoon, are spherical mirrors.

sections.title: SPHERICAL MIRRORS
points: A spherical mirror with its reflecting surface curved inwards (facing the centre of the sphere) is a concave mirror; one curved outwards is a convex mirror.

The pole (P) is the centre of the reflecting surface; the centre of curvature (C) is the centre of the sphere, in front of a concave mirror and behind a convex mirror; the radius of curvature (R) is its radius.
The principal axis is the straight line through the pole and centre of curvature, normal to the mirror at the pole.

Rays parallel to the principal axis meet at (concave) or appear to come from (convex) the principal focus (F); the distance from pole to focus is the focal length (f). A concave mirror focusing sunlight can burn paper.
The diameter of the reflecting surface is the aperture; for mirrors of small aperture R = 2f, so the focus lies midway between pole and centre of curvature.

subsections.title: Image Formation by Spherical Mirrors
points: The nature, position and size of the image formed by a concave mirror depend on the position of the object relative to P, F and C.
An activity with a candle at positions beyond C, at C, between F and C, at F and between P and F records the images; Table 9.1 summarises them.
The image is real for some positions and virtual for one (object between P and F).

subsections.title: Representation of Images Formed by Spherical Mirrors Using Ray Diagrams
points: Each small portion of an extended object acts like a point source; the intersection of at least two reflected rays gives the image position.

Useful rays: a ray parallel to the principal axis passes through (or appears to diverge from) the principal focus; a ray through (or towards) the focus emerges parallel; a ray through (or towards) the centre of curvature returns along the same path; a ray to the pole is reflected obliquely at an equal angle.
Concave mirrors are used in torches, search-lights and vehicle headlights for parallel beams, as shaving mirrors, by dentists, and in solar furnaces.
A convex mirror always gives a virtual, erect, diminished image; a small convex mirror shows a full image of a tall building, as in the wall of Agra Fort facing the Taj Mahal.
Convex mirrors are used as rear-view (wing) mirrors because they give an erect image and a wider field of view.

subsections.title: Sign Convention for Reflection by Spherical Mirrors
points: In the New Cartesian Sign Convention the pole is the origin and the principal axis is the x-axis.
The object is always placed to the left of the mirror, and all distances parallel to the principal axis are measured from the pole.
Distances to the right of the origin are positive and to the left negative; distances above the principal axis are positive and below negative.

subsections.title: Mirror Formula and Magnification
points: Object distance is u, image distance v and focal length f; the mirror formula 1/v + 1/u = 1/f is valid for all spherical mirrors and object positions, using the sign convention.
Magnification m is the ratio of the height of the image to the height of the object, m = h′/h = -v/u.
Object height is positive; image height is positive for virtual and negative for real images, so negative m means a real image and positive m a virtual image.
Example 9.1: a convex rear-view mirror of R = 3.00 m with a bus at 5.00 m gives a virtual, erect image 1.15 m behind the mirror, m = +0.23.
Example 9.2: a 4.0 cm object 25.0 cm from a concave mirror of f = 15.0 cm gives a real, inverted image at 37.5 cm in front, 6.0 cm tall.

sections.title: REFRACTION OF LIGHT
points: The bottom of a pond appears raised, letters under a glass slab appear raised, a pencil in water appears displaced and a lemon in water looks bigger.
The extent of the effect differs for different pairs of media; when travelling obliquely from one medium to another, light changes direction in the second medium, which is refraction of light.
A coin in a bowl hidden from view becomes visible when water is poured in, appearing raised due to refraction.

subsections.title: Refraction through a Rectangular Glass Slab
points: Light entering glass from air (rarer to denser) bends towards the normal; leaving glass to air (denser to rarer) it bends away from the normal.
The emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray because bending at the two parallel faces is equal and opposite, though the ray is shifted sideward slightly.
Refraction is due to change in the speed of light from one medium to another.

Laws of refraction: the incident ray, refracted ray and normal lie in the same plane; sin i / sin r is a constant for a given colour and pair of media (Snell's law), called the refractive index of the second medium with respect to the first.

subsections.title: The Refractive Index
points: Light travels fastest in vacuum at 3×10^8 m s-1, marginally slower in air, and considerably slower in glass or water.
The refractive index of medium 2 with respect to medium 1 is n21 = v1/v2, and n12 = v2/v1.
The absolute refractive index of a medium is nm = c/v; water is 1.33, crown glass 1.52 and diamond 2.42.
The medium with larger refractive index is optically denser; optical density is not mass density, e.g. kerosene is optically denser than water though its mass density is less.

subsections.title: Refraction by Spherical Lenses
points: A lens is a transparent material bound by two surfaces, one or both spherical.
A double convex (convex) lens is thicker in the middle and converges light; a double concave (concave) lens is thicker at the edges and diverges light.
Centres of curvature (C1, C2), principal axis, optical centre (O, through which rays pass undeviated) and aperture are defined; discussion is limited to thin lenses with small apertures.
Parallel rays converge to (convex) or appear to diverge from (concave) the principal focus; a lens has two foci F1 and F2, and the distance from optical centre to focus is the focal length f.

subsections.title: Image Formation by Lenses
points: The image formed by a convex lens for object positions from infinity to between F1 and O is summarised in Table 9.4.
A concave lens always gives a virtual, erect and diminished image, irrespective of the object position (Table 9.5).

subsections.title: Image Formation in Lenses Using Ray Diagrams
points: A ray parallel to the principal axis passes through the focus on the other side of a convex lens or appears to diverge from the focus on the same side of a concave lens.
A ray through a principal focus of a convex lens, or appearing to meet at the focus of a concave lens, emerges parallel to the principal axis.
A ray through the optical centre emerges without any deviation.

subsections.title: Sign Convention for Spherical Lenses
points: The same sign rules as for mirrors apply, but all measurements are taken from the optical centre.
The focal length of a convex lens is positive and that of a concave lens negative.

subsections.title: Lens Formula and Magnification
points: The lens formula 1/v - 1/u = 1/f is valid for any spherical lens with proper signs.
Magnification m = h′/h = v/u.
Example 9.3: a concave lens of f = 15 cm forming an image at 10 cm needs the object at 30 cm; m = +0.33, virtual and erect.
Example 9.4: a 2.0 cm object 15 cm from a convex lens of f = 10 cm gives a real, inverted image at 30 cm on the other side, 4.0 cm tall, m = -2.

subsections.title: Power of a Lens
points: The degree of convergence or divergence of a lens is its power, the reciprocal of its focal length, P = 1/f.
The SI unit of power is the dioptre (D); 1 D is the power of a lens of focal length 1 m, and 1 D = 1 m-1.
Power of a convex lens is positive and of a concave lens negative; +2.0 D means a convex lens of focal length +0.50 m.
The net power of lenses in contact is the algebraic sum P = P1 + P2 + P3 + ..., used by opticians and in cameras, microscopes and telescopes.

bookSummary: Light seems to travel in straight lines.
Mirrors and lenses form images of objects. Images can be either real or virtual, depending on the position of the object.
The reflecting surfaces, of all types, obey the laws of reflection. The refracting surfaces obey the laws of refraction.
New Cartesian Sign Conventions are followed for spherical mirrors and lenses.
Mirror formula, 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, gives the relationship between the object-distance (u), image-distance (v), and focal length (f) of a spherical mirror.
The focal length of a spherical mirror is equal to half its radius of curvature.
The magnification produced by a spherical mirror is the ratio of the height of the image to the height of the object.
A light ray travelling obliquely from a denser medium to a rarer medium bends away from the normal. A light ray bends towards the normal when it travels obliquely from a rarer to a denser medium.
Light travels in vacuum with an enormous speed of 3×10^8 m s-1. The speed of light is different in different media.
The refractive index of a transparent medium is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to that in the medium.
In case of a rectangular glass slab, the refraction takes place at both air-glass interface and glass-air interface. The emergent ray is parallel to the direction of incident ray.
Lens formula, 1/v - 1/u = 1/f, gives the relationship between the object-distance (u), image-distance (v), and the focal length (f) of a spherical lens.
Power of a lens is the reciprocal of its focal length. The SI unit of power of a lens is dioptre.

chapters.title: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
chapters.overview: The chapter applies the ideas of refraction to the human eye: its structure, power of accommodation, and the defects of vision (myopia, hypermetropia, presbyopia) and their correction with lenses. It then studies optical phenomena in nature: refraction through a prism, dispersion of white light and rainbow formation, atmospheric refraction (twinkling of stars, advance sunrise and delayed sunset) and scattering of light (Tyndall effect and the blue colour of the sky).

sections.title: THE HUMAN EYE
points: The human eye is the most significant sense organ because colours cannot be identified with eyes closed.
The eye is like a camera: its lens system forms an image on a light-sensitive screen called the retina; light enters through the cornea, the transparent front bulge.
The eyeball is nearly spherical with a diameter of about 2.3 cm; most refraction occurs at the outer surface of the cornea, and the crystalline lens provides finer adjustment.
The iris, a dark muscular diaphragm, controls the size of the pupil, which regulates light entering the eye.
The eye lens forms an inverted real image on the retina, whose light-sensitive cells send electrical signals via the optic nerves to the brain.

subsections.title: Power of Accommodation
points: The eye lens is fibrous and jelly-like; ciliary muscles modify its curvature and hence focal length.
Relaxed muscles make the lens thin with longer focal length for distant objects; contracted muscles make it thicker with shorter focal length for nearby objects.
The ability of the eye lens to adjust its focal length is accommodation.
The least distance of distinct vision (near point) is about 25 cm for a young adult; the far point of a normal eye is infinity.
In old age the crystalline lens may become milky and cloudy (cataract), causing loss of vision that cataract surgery can restore.

sections.title: DEFECTS OF VISION AND THEIR CORRECTION
points: When the eye gradually loses its power of accommodation, vision becomes blurred due to refractive defects, corrected with suitable spherical lenses.

Myopia (near-sightedness): nearby objects are clear but distant ones are not; the far point is nearer than infinity and the image forms in front of the retina, due to excessive curvature of the eye lens or elongation of the eyeball; corrected by a concave lens.

Hypermetropia (far-sightedness): distant objects are clear but nearby ones are not; the near point is farther than 25 cm and light is focussed behind the retina, because the focal length is too long or the eyeball too small; corrected by a convex lens.

Presbyopia: with ageing the near point recedes, due to weakening ciliary muscles and diminishing lens flexibility; people with both myopia and hypermetropia need bi-focal lenses (concave upper part, convex lower part).
Defects can also be corrected with contact lenses or surgery.
Eye donation: eyes must be removed within 4-6 hours after death; donors can be of any age or sex, and one pair of eyes gives vision to up to four corneal blind people.

sections.title: REFRACTION OF LIGHT THROUGH A PRISM
points: A triangular glass prism has two triangular bases and three rectangular lateral surfaces inclined to each other; the angle between two lateral faces is the angle of the prism.
Tracing a ray with pins shows the incident ray PE, refracted ray EF and emergent ray FS, with angles of incidence, refraction and emergence.
Light bends towards the normal entering glass at the first surface and away from the normal leaving at the second.
The shape of the prism makes the emergent ray bend at an angle to the incident ray, called the angle of deviation.

sections.title: DISPERSION OF WHITE LIGHT BY A GLASS PRISM
points: A prism splits a narrow beam of white light into a band of colours: Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange and Red (VIBGYOR).
The band of coloured components of a light beam is its spectrum, and splitting light into its component colours is dispersion.
Different colours bend through different angles; red bends the least and violet the most.
Isaac Newton first obtained the spectrum of sunlight with a prism; an inverted second prism recombined the colours into white light, showing sunlight is made of seven colours.
A rainbow is a natural spectrum caused by dispersion of sunlight by water droplets, which refract, disperse, internally reflect and refract light again; it forms opposite to the Sun.

sections.title: ATMOSPHERIC REFRACTION
points: Objects seen through hot air above a fire waver because hot air has a slightly lower refractive index and conditions keep changing; this is atmospheric refraction on a small scale.
Twinkling of stars: starlight is refracted continuously in the atmosphere, so a star appears slightly higher than its actual position and its apparent position and brightness fluctuate.
Planets do not twinkle because they are closer and act as extended sources, so variations from their many point sources average out.
Advance sunrise and delayed sunset: the Sun is visible about 2 minutes before actual sunrise and 2 minutes after actual sunset due to atmospheric refraction, which also flattens the Sun's disc.

sections.title: SCATTERING OF LIGHT
points: The blue sky, colour of deep sea water and reddening of the Sun at sunrise and sunset arise from the interplay of light with matter.
A light beam's path is invisible in a true solution but visible in a colloidal solution with larger particles.

subsections.title: Tyndall Effect
points: The atmosphere is a heterogeneous mixture of smoke, water droplets, dust and air molecules; light striking these fine particles makes the beam's path visible.
Scattering of light by colloidal particles gives the Tyndall effect, seen in a beam entering a smoke-filled room or sunlight through a dense forest canopy.
Very fine particles scatter mainly blue light, larger particles scatter longer wavelengths, and large enough particles make scattered light appear white.

subsections.title: Why is the colour of the clear Sky Blue?
points: Air molecules and fine particles, smaller than the wavelength of visible light, scatter shorter blue wavelengths more strongly than red; red light has a wavelength about 1.8 times that of blue.
The scattered blue light enters our eyes; without an atmosphere the sky would look dark, as it does to passengers at very high altitudes.
Danger signal lights are red because red is least scattered by fog or smoke and can be seen at a distance.

keyTerms.meaning: A delicate light-sensitive membrane with an enormous number of light-sensitive cells, on which the eye lens forms an image.
The thin transparent membrane forming the bulge on the front of the eyeball, through which light enters.
A dark muscular diaphragm behind the cornea that controls the size of the pupil.
The opening that regulates and controls the amount of light entering the eye.
Muscles that modify the curvature of the eye lens.
The ability of the eye lens to adjust its focal length.

keyTerms.term: Near point (least distance of distinct vision)
keyTerms.meaning: The minimum distance at which objects can be seen most distinctly without strain; about 25 cm for a young adult.
The farthest point up to which the eye can see objects clearly; infinity for a normal eye.
A condition in which the crystalline lens becomes milky and cloudy, causing partial or complete loss of vision.
Near-sightedness: nearby objects are seen clearly but distant objects are not.
Far-sightedness: distant objects are seen clearly but nearby objects are not.
The defect in which the near point gradually recedes with ageing, due to weakening ciliary muscles and less flexible eye lens.
Lenses with a concave upper portion for distant vision and a convex lower part for near vision.
The angle between two lateral faces of a prism.
The angle at which the emergent ray bends relative to the direction of the incident ray.
The band of the coloured components of a light beam.
The splitting of light into its component colours.
Any light that gives a spectrum similar to that of sunlight.

keyResults.statement: The eyeball is approximately spherical with a diameter of about 2.3 cm.

keyResults.label: Range of normal vision
keyResults.statement: A normal eye can see objects clearly between 25 cm (near point) and infinity (far point).

keyResults.label: Correction of defects
keyResults.statement: Myopia is corrected by a concave lens of suitable power; hypermetropia by a convex lens of suitable power; bi-focal lenses for both.

keyResults.statement: Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red (VIBGYOR); red bends the least and violet the most.

keyResults.statement: The Sun is visible about 2 minutes before actual sunrise and about 2 minutes after actual sunset.

bookSummary: The ability of the eye to focus on both near and distant objects, by adjusting its focal length, is called the accommodation of the eye.

The smallest distance, at which the eye can see objects clearly without strain, is called the near point of the eye or the least distance of distinct vision. For a young adult with normal vision, it is about 25 cm.

The common refractive defects of vision include myopia, hypermetropia and presbyopia. Myopia (short-sightedness – the image of distant objects is focussed before the retina) is corrected by using a concave lens of suitable power. Hypermetropia (far-sightedness – the image of nearby objects is focussed beyond the retina) is corrected by using a convex lens of suitable power. The eye loses its power of accommodation at old age.
The splitting of white light into its component colours is called dispersion.
Scattering of light causes the blue colour of sky.

chapters.title: Electricity
chapters.overview: The chapter explains electric current and circuits, electric potential and potential difference, and circuit diagrams with standard symbols. It develops Ohm's law, the factors on which resistance depends (length, area of cross-section, material and resistivity), and resistors in series and parallel. It then covers the heating effect of electric current (Joule's law) and its applications such as bulbs and fuses, and electric power and energy, with many worked examples.

sections.title: ELECTRIC CURRENT AND CIRCUIT
points: Flow of electric charge through a conductor is an electric current; a switch makes a conducting link, and a continuous and closed path of current is an electric circuit.
Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charges; in metallic wires electrons carry the charge, but conventionally current direction is opposite to electron flow.
If net charge Q flows in time t, current I = Q/t; the SI unit of charge is the coulomb, equivalent to the charge of nearly 6 × 10^18 electrons (electron charge 1.6 × 10^-19 C).
Current is measured in amperes (1 A = 1 C/1 s), with milliampere and microampere for small currents, using an ammeter always connected in series.
Example 11.1: 0.5 A for 10 minutes gives a charge of 300 C.

sections.title: ELECTRIC POTENTIAL AND POTENTIAL DIFFERENCE
points: Like water needing a pressure difference, electrons move only if there is a potential difference along the conductor, produced by a battery of one or more cells through chemical action.
The cell expends its stored chemical energy to maintain the current.
Potential difference between two points is the work done to move a unit charge from one to the other, V = W/Q.
The SI unit is the volt, named after Alessandro Volta; 1 V = 1 J C-1, measured by a voltmeter always connected in parallel.
Example 11.2: moving 2 C across 12 V takes 24 J of work.

sections.title: CIRCUIT DIAGRAM
points: An electric circuit comprises a cell or battery, a plug key, electrical components and connecting wires.

A schematic circuit diagram uses conventional symbols (Table 11.1) for a cell, battery, open and closed key, wire joint, wires crossing without joining, bulb, resistor, rheostat, ammeter and voltmeter.

sections.title: OHM’S LAW
points: Measuring current and potential difference for a nichrome wire with one to four cells gives nearly the same V/I each time, and the V–I graph is a straight line through the origin.
Georg Simon Ohm (1787–1854) found in 1827 that the potential difference across a metallic wire is directly proportional to the current through it, provided its temperature remains the same.
V/I = R, the resistance, the property of a conductor to resist the flow of charges; its SI unit is the ohm (Ω), 1 Ω = 1 V/1 A.
I = V/R, so current is inversely proportional to resistance; a rheostat is used to change resistance and regulate current.
Different components draw different currents; electrons are restrained by atoms, so a conductor of appreciable resistance is a resistor, and insulators offer even higher resistance.

sections.title: FACTORS ON WHICH THE RESISTANCE OF A CONDUCTOR DEPENDS
points: Doubling a wire's length halves the current; a thicker wire of the same material increases current; a different material changes it.
Resistance of a uniform metallic conductor is directly proportional to its length and inversely proportional to its area of cross-section: R = ρl/A, where ρ is the electrical resistivity (unit Ω m).
Metals and alloys have resistivity of 10^-8 to 10^-6 Ω m; insulators like rubber and glass 10^12 to 10^17 Ω m; both resistance and resistivity vary with temperature.

Alloys have higher resistivity than their constituent metals and do not oxidise readily, so are used in heating devices; tungsten is used for bulb filaments and copper and aluminium for transmission lines.

Examples 11.3 to 11.6 calculate currents drawn by a bulb and heater, current at a doubled voltage, the resistivity of a manganese wire, and the resistance of a wire of half length and double area (1 Ω).

sections.title: RESISTANCE OF A SYSTEM OF RESISTORS
points: Resistors can be joined end to end (in series) or between two common points (in parallel), and Ohm's law is applied to such combinations.

subsections.title: Resistors in Series
points: In a series combination the current is the same in every part of the circuit.
The total potential difference equals the sum of potential differences across individual resistors, V = V1 + V2 + V3.
The equivalent resistance is Rs = R1 + R2 + R3, greater than any individual resistance.
Example 11.7: a 20 Ω lamp and 4 Ω conductor on 6 V give 24 Ω total, 0.25 A, and 5 V and 1 V across them.

subsections.title: Resistors in Parallel
points: In parallel the potential difference across each resistor is the same, and the total current is the sum of branch currents, I = I1 + I2 + I3.
The reciprocal of the equivalent resistance equals the sum of reciprocals: 1/Rp = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3.
Example 11.8: 5 Ω, 10 Ω and 30 Ω in parallel on 12 V draw 2.4 A, 1.2 A and 0.4 A, total 4 A, Rp = 3 Ω; Example 11.9 combines series and parallel groups to get 18 Ω and 0.67 A.

Series circuits are impractical for a bulb and heater needing different currents, and one failed component breaks the whole circuit (as with fairy lights); parallel circuits divide current and reduce total resistance.

sections.title: HEATING EFFECT OF ELECTRIC CURRENT
points: Part of a source's energy may do useful work and the rest raises the temperature of the gadget; in a purely resistive circuit the energy is dissipated entirely as heat, the heating effect of electric current.
Power input P = VQ/t = VI, and heat produced in time t is H = VIt.
Using Ohm's law, H = I²Rt, which is Joule's law of heating: heat is proportional to the square of current, to resistance and to time.
Example 11.10 finds the current and resistance of an electric iron at 840 W and 360 W; Example 11.11 finds 20 V across a 4 Ω resistor producing 100 J each second.

subsections.title: Practical Applications of Heating Effect of Electric Current
points: Heating is often undesirable, but is used in the electric iron, toaster, oven, kettle and heater.

In an electric bulb the filament of tungsten (melting point 3380°C) gets very hot and emits light; bulbs are filled with nitrogen and argon to prolong filament life, and most power still appears as heat.
A fuse, placed in series with the device, has a wire of appropriate melting point that melts and breaks the circuit when current exceeds the specified value.
Domestic fuses are rated 1 A, 2 A, 3 A, 5 A, 10 A, etc.; a 1 kW iron at 220 V draws 4.54 A and needs a 5 A fuse.

sections.title: ELECTRIC POWER
points: The rate at which electric energy is dissipated or consumed is electric power, P = VI = I²R = V²/R.
The SI unit is the watt: 1 W = 1 V × 1 A; a larger unit is the kilowatt (1000 W).
Electric energy is measured in watt hour; the commercial unit is the kilowatt hour ('unit'), 1 kW h = 3.6 × 10^6 J.
Electrons are not consumed in a circuit; we pay for the energy used to move them.
Example 11.12: a bulb on 220 V drawing 0.50 A has power 110 W; Example 11.13: a 400 W refrigerator for 8 hours a day for 30 days uses 96 kW h costing Rs 288 at Rs 3.00 per kW h.

bookSummary: A stream of electrons moving through a conductor constitutes an electric current. Conventionally, the direction of current is taken opposite to the direction of flow of electrons.
The SI unit of electric current is ampere.
To set the electrons in motion in an electric circuit, we use a cell or a battery. A cell generates a potential difference across its terminals. It is measured in volts (V).
Resistance is a property that resists the flow of electrons in a conductor. It controls the magnitude of the current. The SI unit of resistance is ohm (Ω).
Ohm's law: The potential difference across the ends of a resistor is directly proportional to the current through it, provided its temperature remains the same.
The resistance of a conductor depends directly on its length, inversely on its area of cross-section, and also on the material of the conductor.
The equivalent resistance of several resistors in series is equal to the sum of their individual resistances.
A set of resistors connected in parallel has an equivalent resistance Rp given by 1/Rp = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3 + ...
The electrical energy dissipated in a resistor is given by W = V × I × t.
The unit of power is watt (W). One watt of power is consumed when 1 A of current flows at a potential difference of 1 V.
The commercial unit of electrical energy is kilowatt hour (kWh). 1 kW h = 3,600,000 J = 3.6 × 10^6 J.

chapters.title: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current
chapters.overview: The chapter shows that an electric current produces a magnetic effect, linking electricity and magnetism. It describes magnetic fields and field lines of a bar magnet, the magnetic field due to current through a straight conductor (with the right-hand thumb rule), a circular loop and a solenoid, and electromagnets. It then explains the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field (Fleming's left-hand rule) and domestic electric circuits with their safety measures such as earthing and fuses.

sections.title: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current
points: A compass needle placed near a copper wire is deflected when current passes, showing that current produces a magnetic effect and that electricity and magnetism are linked.
Hans Christian Oersted (1777–1851) accidentally discovered this in 1820; the unit of magnetic field strength, the oersted, is named after him.

sections.title: MAGNETIC FIELD AND FIELD LINES
points: A compass needle is a small bar magnet; its north-seeking end is the north pole and south-seeking end the south pole; like poles repel and unlike poles attract.
Iron filings around a bar magnet arrange in a pattern because the magnet exerts a force in the surrounding region, the magnetic field; the lines they follow are magnetic field lines.
Field lines can also be drawn step by step with a compass; deflection increases towards the poles.
Magnetic field has direction and magnitude; field lines emerge from the north pole and merge at the south pole, run from south to north inside the magnet, and are closed curves.
The field is stronger where field lines are crowded, and no two field lines cross, since a compass cannot point in two directions.

sections.title: MAGNETIC FIELD DUE TO A CURRENT-CARRYING CONDUCTOR
points: An electric current through a metallic conductor produces a magnetic field around it, whose pattern depends on the shape of the conductor.

subsections.title: Magnetic Field due to a Current through a Straight Conductor
points: With current north to south in a wire over a compass, the north pole deflects east; reversing the current reverses the deflection, so the field direction reverses.
Iron filings around a vertical current-carrying wire form concentric circles, which represent the magnetic field lines.
Increasing the current increases the deflection, so the field at a point increases with current.
The field decreases as distance from the wire increases, and the concentric circles become larger away from the wire.

subsections.title: Right-Hand Thumb Rule
points: Holding a current-carrying straight conductor in the right hand with the thumb along the current, the fingers wrap around it in the direction of the field lines.
It is also called Maxwell's corkscrew rule: the rotation of a corkscrew driven along the current gives the field direction.
Example 12.1: for a power line with current east to west, the field turns clockwise viewed from the east end and anti-clockwise viewed from the west end.

subsections.title: Magnetic Field due to a Current through a Circular Loop
points: Around every point of a circular loop the field circles grow larger away from the wire, and at the centre the arcs appear as straight lines.
Every section of the loop contributes field lines in the same direction within the loop.
A coil of n turns produces a field n times as large as a single turn because the fields of the turns add up.

subsections.title: Magnetic Field due to a Current in a Solenoid
points: A coil of many circular turns of insulated copper wire wrapped closely in the shape of a cylinder is a solenoid.
Its field pattern is similar to a bar magnet's, with one end behaving as a north pole and the other as a south pole.
Field lines inside are parallel straight lines, so the field is uniform inside the solenoid.
The strong field inside can magnetise soft iron placed in the coil, forming an electromagnet.

sections.title: FORCE ON A CURRENT-CARRYING CONDUCTOR IN A MAGNETIC FIELD
points: Andre Marie Ampere (1775–1836) suggested a magnet exerts an equal and opposite force on a current-carrying conductor.
An aluminium rod between the poles of a horse-shoe magnet is displaced when current flows; reversing the current or the field reverses the force.
The force is largest when the current is at right angles to the magnetic field, and is then perpendicular to both.

Fleming's left-hand rule: with thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the left hand mutually perpendicular, the first finger points along the field, the second along the current, and the thumb along the force.

Electric motors, generators, loudspeakers, microphones and measuring instruments use current-carrying conductors and magnetic fields; Example 12.2 shows an electron's force is into the page since current is opposite to electron motion.
Weak magnetic fields produced in the heart and brain form the basis of Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) used in medical diagnosis.

sections.title: DOMESTIC ELECTRIC CIRCUITS
points: Homes receive power through the mains; the live wire has red insulation, the neutral wire black, and the potential difference between them in India is 220 V.
The wires pass through a main fuse into an electricity meter and through the main switch to line wires; separate circuits of 15 A (geysers, air coolers) and 5 A (bulbs, fans) are often used.
The earth wire with green insulation connects to a metal plate deep in the earth, giving a low-resistance path so leakage to a metallic body does not give a severe shock.
Appliances are connected in parallel so each has equal potential difference, each with its own switch.

Overloading can occur by short-circuiting (live and neutral wires in direct contact), an accidental hike in supply voltage, or too many appliances on one socket; the fuse melts by Joule heating to break the circuit.

bookSummary: A compass needle is a small magnet. Its one end, which points towards north, is called a north pole, and the other end, which points towards south, is called a south pole.
A magnetic field exists in the region surrounding a magnet, in which the force of the magnet can be detected.

Field lines are used to represent a magnetic field. A field line is the path along which a hypothetical free north pole would tend to move. The direction of the magnetic field at a point is given by the direction that a north pole placed at that point would take. Field lines are shown closer together where the magnetic field is greater.

A metallic wire carrying an electric current has associated with it a magnetic field. The field lines about the wire consist of a series of concentric circles whose direction is given by the right-hand rule.

The pattern of the magnetic field around a conductor due to an electric current flowing through it depends on the shape of the conductor. The magnetic field of a solenoid carrying a current is similar to that of a bar magnet.
An electromagnet consists of a core of soft iron wrapped around with a coil of insulated copper wire.

A current-carrying conductor when placed in a magnetic field experiences a force. If the direction of the field and that of the current are mutually perpendicular to each other, then the force acting on the conductor will be perpendicular to both and will be given by Fleming's left-hand rule.

In our houses we receive AC electric power of 220 V with a frequency of 50 Hz. One of the wires in this supply is with red insulation, called live wire. The other one is of black insulation, which is a neutral wire. The potential difference between the two is 220 V. The third is the earth wire that has green insulation and this is connected to a metallic body deep inside earth. It is used as a safety measure to ensure that any leakage of current to a metallic body does not give any severe shock to a user.
Fuse is the most important safety device, used for protecting the circuits due to short-circuiting or overloading of the circuits.

chapters.title: Our Environment
chapters.overview: The chapter studies how components of the environment interact and how human activities affect it. It describes ecosystems and their biotic and abiotic components, producers, consumers and decomposers, food chains and webs, trophic levels, the unidirectional flow of energy with the 10% rule, and biological magnification. It then examines two environmental problems: depletion of the ozone layer by CFCs and the management of biodegradable and non-biodegradable waste.

sections.title: Our Environment
points: The word 'environment' is often used on television, in newspapers and at global summits on environmental issues.
The chapter studies how components of the environment interact with each other and how we impact the environment.

sections.title: ECO-SYSTEM — WHAT ARE ITS COMPONENTS?
points: All interacting organisms in an area together with the non-living constituents of the environment form an ecosystem, with biotic components (living organisms) and abiotic components (temperature, rainfall, wind, soil, minerals).
Forests, ponds and lakes are natural ecosystems; gardens, crop-fields and aquariums are human-made (artificial) ecosystems.
Producers are green plants and certain bacteria that make food by photosynthesis; consumers (herbivores, carnivores, omnivores, parasites) depend on producers directly or indirectly.
Decomposers, bacteria and fungi, break down dead remains and wastes into simple inorganic substances that return to the soil for plants.

subsections.title: Food Chains and Webs
points: A series of organisms feeding on one another forms a food chain, and each step is a trophic level: producers first, herbivores (primary consumers) second, small carnivores (secondary consumers) third and larger carnivores (tertiary consumers) fourth.
Green plants capture about 1% of sunlight falling on their leaves; on average 10% of food eaten is turned into body mass and made available to the next level.
Because so little energy passes on, food chains generally have only three or four steps, and the greatest number of individuals is at the producer level.
Organisms are eaten by several kinds of organisms, so relationships form branching food webs.
Energy flow is unidirectional and the energy available diminishes progressively at each trophic level.
Non-degradable pesticides entering the food chain accumulate progressively at each trophic level, with maximum concentration in humans at the top; this is biological magnification.

sections.title: HOW DO OUR ACTIVITIES AFFECT THE ENVIRONMENT?
points: Changes in the environment affect us and our activities change the environment.
Two problems are examined in detail: depletion of the ozone layer and waste disposal.

subsections.title: Ozone Layer and How it is Getting Depleted
points: Ozone (O3) is a molecule of three oxygen atoms; it is a deadly poison but at higher levels of the atmosphere it shields the earth from ultraviolet (UV) radiation, which causes skin cancer.
UV radiation splits O2 into free oxygen atoms, which combine with O2 to form ozone.
Ozone began to drop sharply in the 1980s, linked to chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) used as refrigerants and in fire extinguishers.
In 1987 UNEP forged an agreement to freeze CFC production at 1986 levels, and CFC-free refrigerators are now mandatory worldwide.

subsections.title: Managing the Garbage we Produce
points: Enzymes are specific in action, so many human-made materials like plastics are not broken down by bacteria or saprophytes and persist for a long time.
Substances broken down by biological processes are biodegradable; those not broken down are non-biodegradable and may persist or harm the ecosystem.
Improved life-styles, disposable items and changes in packaging have increased waste, much of it non-biodegradable.
Disposable cups in trains: plastic cups, then clay kulhads (which would lose fertile top-soil), and now paper cups show the trade-offs in managing waste.
Activities examine how homes, local bodies, sewage systems and industries handle waste, and how electronic items and plastics are disposed of or recycled.

bookSummary: The various components of an ecosystem are interdependent.
The producers make the energy from sunlight available to the rest of the ecosystem.
There is a loss of energy as we go from one trophic level to the next, this limits the number of trophic levels in a food-chain.
Human activities have an impact on the environment.
The use of chemicals like CFCs has endangered the ozone layer. Since the ozone layer protects against the ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, this could damage the environment.
The waste we generate may be biodegradable or non-biodegradable.
The disposal of the waste we generate is causing serious environmental problems.
